apollo11-lm.caption: Buzz Aldrin walks beside Eagle's landing leg on 20 July 1969. Neil Armstrong took this photo with a Hasselblad camera.
A bootprint in the fine, powdery Moon dust at Tranquility Base, photographed to study how the soil packs down.
Buzz Aldrin stands beside the U.S. flag. Eagle's landing leg and footprints are all around.

apollo12-lm.caption: Two spacecraft on the Moon: Pete Conrad checks old Surveyor 3, with the Apollo 12 lander Intrepid on the horizon, 20 November 1969.
Pete Conrad beside the flag on the Ocean of Storms during the first moonwalk, 19 November 1969.
Alan Bean by the tool carrier. Look closely: Pete Conrad, who took the photo, is reflected in Bean's visor.

surveyor3.caption: Surveyor 3's own TV camera looks at its round footpad on 20 April 1967. The mark beside it shows where the lander bounced while landing.
Surveyor 3's scoop reaches out to dig the first trench on the Moon, 21 April 1967.

apollo14-lm.caption: The lander Antares with a jewel-like sun flare, seen during the first Apollo 14 moonwalk on 5 February 1971.
Alan Shepard, the first American in space, stands by the flag at Fra Mauro, 5 February 1971.
Edgar Mitchell next to the two-wheeled cart the crew pulled across the Moon, 6 February 1971.

apollo15-lm.caption: Jim Irwin salutes the flag at Hadley Base, with the lander Falcon and the rover nearby, 1 August 1971.
A telephoto view across Hadley Rille, a winding valley on the Moon. The far wall is almost 2 km away.
Mount Hadley, a Moon mountain about 4.5 km tall, seen from the Apollo 15 science station.

apollo15-lrv.caption: Jim Irwin works at the rover during the first drive of a car on the Moon, 31 July 1971.
David Scott at the rover, parked on the edge of Hadley Rille, 31 July 1971.

apollo16-lm.caption: John Young jumps while saluting the flag. Orion and the rover are on the left, Stone Mountain behind, 21 April 1972.
The lander Orion and the rover in the Descartes highlands, during the first Apollo 16 moonwalk.
Charlie Duke collects rocks on the rim of Plum Crater, with the rover parked behind him.

apollo16-lrv.caption: John Young drives the rover to its final parking place on 23 April 1972. The big shadow is the lander.
John Young puts tools back on the rover during the second Apollo 16 moonwalk, 22 April 1972.

apollo17-lm.caption: Harrison Schmitt beside the flag, with Earth hanging in the black sky above, December 1972.
Harrison Schmitt next to a huge split boulder during the last moonwalk of Apollo, 13 December 1972.

apollo17-lrv.caption: Earth floats above the rover's dish antenna while Gene Cernan stands beside it, 13 December 1972.
The rover's broken fender, fixed with maps and clamps after a hammer knocked part of it off.

surveyor1.caption: Surveyor 1's long shadow on the Moon in the late afternoon, June 1966. It was the first U.S. soft landing on the Moon.
Surveyor 1 looks at its own footpad, which barely sank into the ground. This proved the Moon was firm enough for Apollo.
A self-portrait: Surveyor 1's camera looks at part of the lander during its first day on the Moon.

surveyor5.caption: Surveyor 5's footpad in the soil. The trench beside it formed when the foot slid while landing, September 1967.
A close-up of the furrow dug by Surveyor 5's footpad as it landed on 10 September 1967.

surveyor6.caption: Surveyor 6 made the first 'hop' on the Moon. This shows its first landing marks, blasted by its rocket engines when it took off again.
A panorama of the flat plain of Sinus Medii around Surveyor 6, November 1967.

surveyor7.caption: The rocky land near Tycho crater, January 1968. The hills on the horizon are about 13 km away.
A faint glow along the Moon's horizon after sunset. Scientists think it is dust floating just above the ground.

ranger7.caption: The first picture of the Moon taken by a U.S. spacecraft, 31 July 1964, about 17 minutes before Ranger 7 crashed on purpose.
Guericke crater, 63 km wide, 8.5 minutes before impact. Ranger 7 was about 1,335 km above the Moon.

ranger8.caption: The craters Ritter and Sabine from 302 km up, two and a half minutes before Ranger 8 hit the Moon on 20 February 1965.

ranger9.caption: The Moon's surface photographed by Ranger 9 as it dived into Alphonsus crater on 24 March 1965. People watched its pictures live on TV.

lcross-ssc.caption: LCROSS tests its visible-light camera on the Moon while swinging past it in June 2009.
The target inside dark Cabeus crater, seen by LCROSS minutes before its rocket stage hit, 9 October 2009.
The tiny white spot is the flash of the rocket stage hitting Cabeus, seen by LCROSS's heat-sensing camera just before LCROSS hit too.

grail-ebb.caption: A view of the Moon's surface taken by the MoonKAM camera on Ebb. School students chose where to point it.
Craters seen by Ebb's MoonKAM camera in 2012, as part of a project run for middle-school students.
More of the Moon from Ebb's MoonKAM, which took thousands of pictures requested by classrooms.

viking1.caption: The very first photo taken on the surface of Mars, minutes after Viking 1 landed on 20 July 1976. Rocks and dust lie next to the lander's footpad.
Viking 1's first colour picture of Mars, July 1976: a rocky, rusty-red plain under a pinkish sky.

viking2.caption: The first colour view of the Viking 2 landing site in Utopia Planitia, September 1976. The ground is covered in rocks.
A thin layer of white frost on the ground around Viking 2 during the Martian winter.

pathfinder.caption: Sunset over the Twin Peaks hills, one minute after the Sun went down, August 1997. Dust high in the air keeps the sky glowing.
Pathfinder's camera watches little Sojourner press its instrument against a rock nicknamed Yogi, July 1997.

sojourner.caption: Sojourner's front camera looks back at its lander, with the ramp it drove down, on its 6th day on Mars (July 1997).
On day 70, Sojourner looks at the rock Yogi. Its own wheel cleats show at the bottom left.

spirit.caption: The McMurdo panorama: a 360-degree view from the small hill where Spirit spent the Martian winter of 2006. Its own deck and solar panels are in the middle.
The Sun sets behind the rim of Gusev crater on 19 May 2005, photographed by Spirit's Pancam.
Spirit says goodbye to Home Plate, a flat plateau of layered volcanic rock it explored in 2006.

opportunity.caption: Opportunity's last panorama, made from 354 Pancam pictures between 13 May and 10 June 2018, just before a huge dust storm ended its mission.
Looking down Perseverance Valley on the inner slope of Endeavour Crater, with Opportunity's own wheel tracks, autumn 2017.
Victoria Crater seen from the cliff called Cape Verde, about 800 m across, photographed in 2006.

phoenix.caption: Lumps of ice in a trench Phoenix dug, 15 June 2008. A few days later they had vanished into the thin air: proof they were water ice.
A full circle around Phoenix on the flat arctic plain of Mars, made from more than 400 pictures.
Morning frost inside a trench dug by Phoenix, on its 113th day (September 2008), as Martian winter came.

insight.caption: InSight's first picture, taken minutes after landing on 26 November 2018. The dusty spots are on its protective lens cover.
A Martian sunset seen by the camera on InSight's robot arm, 25 April 2019.
InSight's final selfie, 24 April 2022. Its solar panels are covered in dust, which slowly cut off its power.

ingenuity.caption: Ingenuity's own shadow, photographed while hovering on 19 April 2021: the first powered, controlled flight on another planet.
The first colour picture taken from the air on Mars, on flight 2 (22 April 2021), from 5.2 m up. The stripes are Perseverance's wheel tracks.
After flight 72 in January 2024, Ingenuity photographed the shadow of a damaged rotor blade. It never flew again.

curiosity.caption: Mount Sharp, the 5 km-tall mountain Curiosity is climbing. Colours are adjusted to look like Earth daylight, which makes the sky look too blue.
A blue sunset in Gale Crater, 15 April 2015. Fine Martian dust lets blue light through near the Sun.
Home seen from Mars: the brightest dot, a little left of centre, is Earth, with our Moon just below it. Twilight on 31 January 2014.
Inside the Gediz Vallis channel, September 2024. The panorama is stitched from 341 Mastcam pictures.

perseverance.caption: Perseverance's first 360-degree panorama, from 142 Mastcam-Z pictures taken on its third day on Mars (21 February 2021).
A selfie with the Ingenuity helicopter, 6 April 2021, stitched from 62 pictures taken by the camera on the rover's arm.
The rock "Cheyava Falls", 18 July 2024. Its tiny "leopard spots" are one of the best clues yet that Mars may once have had life (it is still being studied).

pioneer10.caption: Jupiter photographed by Pioneer 10 from 2.6 million km on 2 December 1973, during the first visit to the giant planet. A moon shows at upper right.
Jupiter's clouds and the Great Red Spot, a storm bigger than Earth, from Pioneer 10's 1973 flyby.

pioneer11.caption: The first look at Jupiter from above, near its north pole, taken by Pioneer 11 in December 1974.
Saturn and its moon Titan, photographed by Pioneer 11, the first spacecraft to visit Saturn, in 1979.

voyager1.caption: The Pale Blue Dot (2020 remastered version). On 14 February 1990, from about 6 billion km away, Voyager 1 looked back: Earth is the tiny speck in the sunbeam on the right.
The first picture of Earth and the Moon together in one frame, taken by Voyager 1 on 18 September 1977, 11.7 million km from home.
Jupiter with its moons Io (above the Great Red Spot) and Europa, 13 February 1979.

voyager2.caption: A thin crescent of Uranus, a view nobody had seen before Voyager 2 flew past it in January 1986.
Neptune with its Great Dark Spot storm, August 1989. Voyager 2 is still the only spacecraft to visit Neptune.
Leaving Neptune behind: the crescents of Neptune and its moon Triton, three days after the closest approach in 1989.
Triton, Neptune's largest moon, 22 August 1989. Its icy south pole was having summer.

newhorizons.caption: Pluto on 14 July 2015, with its colours boosted to show different kinds of ice. The pale heart shape is a giant plain of frozen nitrogen.
Looking back 15 minutes after the flyby: icy mountains up to 3.5 km tall, flat ice plains and layers of haze in Pluto's sky.
Arrokoth, a snowman-shaped object in the Kuiper Belt, visited on 1 January 2019: the farthest world any spacecraft has explored.
On its way to Pluto in 2007, New Horizons caught a giant volcanic plume rising from Jupiter's moon Io.

juno.caption: Jupiter's north pole, never seen this clearly before, photographed by JunoCam on 27 August 2016.
Ganymede, the largest moon in the Solar System, from about 1,000 km away on 7 June 2021 (green filter, so it looks black and white).
Cracks and ridges in Europa's ice shell, taken by Juno's star-tracking camera on 29 September 2022.

galileo.caption: Jupiter's icy moon Europa, made from Galileo pictures from the late 1990s. An ocean is thought to hide under the cracked ice.
Io in true colour, the most volcanic world in the Solar System. Its yellow and orange colours come from sulfur.
Asteroid Ida and its tiny moon Dactyl (the dot on the right), 28 August 1993: the first moon ever found around an asteroid. Colours are enhanced.

cassini.caption: "The Day the Earth Smiled", 19 July 2013: Saturn and its rings, lit from behind. Earth is the tiny bright dot below the rings, lower right.
Saturn's six-sided "hexagon" storm around its north pole, in November 2012 (top) and September 2016 (bottom). Its colour changed with Saturn's seasons.
Jets of ice spraying out of the south pole of the moon Enceladus, from an ocean under its surface.
Lakes and seas of liquid methane near the north pole of Titan, seen on one of Cassini's last visits in 2017.

messenger.caption: A side of Mercury that no spacecraft had ever seen, photographed on MESSENGER's first flyby, 14 January 2008.
The first picture ever taken from orbit around Mercury, 29 March 2011 (colours from three camera filters).
Mercury in false colours, which show the different kinds of rock. To your eyes it would look grey.

magellan.caption: Venus's surface, mapped by Magellan's radar, which can see through the thick clouds. Gaps are filled with older Pioneer Venus data.
Maat Mons, a giant volcano on Venus, shown in 3-D using radar data. The heights are stretched to make it easier to see.

pioneer_venus_orbiter.caption: Venus's clouds photographed in ultraviolet light on 5 February 1979. In ordinary light they look almost plain white.
Ultraviolet view of Venus on 26 February 1979, showing the big Y-shaped cloud pattern that keeps forming again and again.

dawn.caption: The giant asteroid Vesta, full of craters and grooves, from 5,200 km on 24 July 2011.
The dwarf planet Ceres on 5-6 May 2015, from 13,600 km. The bright spots are salty deposits.
Close-up of the bright spots of Occator Crater on Ceres, from Dawn's lowest orbit in 2016.

near_shoemaker.caption: Asteroid Mathilde, the first picture NEAR took of it during a flyby in June 1997.
Asteroid Eros, shaped like a giant peanut about 33 km long. NEAR's first whole-Eros mosaic from orbit, 2000.

kepler.caption: Kepler's first full picture of its star field in Cygnus and Lyra, April 2009. It watched these stars for years, looking for planets.
A zoom into the same picture. The star in the centre has a known giant planet, TrES-2b, that circles it every 2.5 days.

spitzer.caption: The crowded centre of our Milky Way galaxy in infrared light, which shines through dust that hides it from our eyes.
The Andromeda galaxy in infrared light. Blue shows starlight, red-orange shows dust (the background includes WISE data).
The Eagle Nebula, a cloud where new stars are born, seen in infrared light.

deep_impact_impactor.caption: Comet Tempel 1 about 5 minutes before the impactor hit it, 4 July 2005, taken by the impactor's own camera.
About 30 seconds before impact: craters and smooth patches on the comet's icy surface.

stardust.caption: Comet Wild 2 on 2 January 2004, the closest short-exposure picture from Stardust as it collected comet dust to bring home.
Jets of gas and dust spraying from comet Wild 2, made by laying a long-exposure picture over a short one from the same flyby.

dart.caption: Asteroid Didymos (big) and its moonlet Dimorphos, about 2.5 minutes before DART crashed into Dimorphos on 26 September 2022.
Dimorphos 11 seconds before impact, from 68 km away. The crash changed its orbit: the first test of pushing an asteroid.

osiris_apex.caption: Asteroid Bennu, a rubble pile about 500 m wide, in a mosaic of OSIRIS-REx pictures.
The moment of "touch-and-go" on Bennu, 20 October 2020, when the spacecraft grabbed rock and dust to bring to Earth.
